talks.title: Last Night A DJ Erased My Drive: A Journey Through Cybersecurity, Chaos, And Control
talks.teaser: Uses music history and production analogies to explain how identity-driven attacks blend into normal activity and evade detection.
talks.summary:
Mathew Caplan builds the talk around an analogy between music and cyber security, arguing that both start with a trigger, unfold over time and depend on timing and rhythm. He compares a security stack to a recording studio, where threats are the signal, alerts and false positives are the noise, and the architecture is the mix. Early sections survey how music has been used as propaganda, as a tool of coercion and as a form of resistance, from coded songs to bootleg records cut from discarded X-ray film.

The middle of the talk turns to modern attacks. Caplan covers AI-generated tracks and streaming fraud as an example of abuse at scale, then walks through the 2020 SolarWinds supply chain compromise and the 2024 Live Nation data breach, where stolen credentials and missing multi-factor authentication let attackers log in as trusted users in a third-party environment. The common thread is that identity-driven intrusions look like routine activity, move slowly and stay below alert thresholds for long periods.

For practitioners, the closing recommendations include zero trust with continuous checks on identity and context, reducing noise through least privilege and segmentation, and managing third-party risk with priority on critical suppliers. He advises detecting attack sequences rather than isolated events, scoring alerts by risk, correlating signals across domains, and running purple teaming against realistic scenarios so that detections are actually tested. The main message is that simpler architecture and pattern-based detection matter more than chasing every signal.

talks.title: Beyond Cognitive Bias And Digital Literacy
talks.teaser: Argues that trauma and attachment research can explain social engineering vulnerability better than cognitive bias models.
talks.summary:
The talk questions the common explanation that people fall for social engineering because they lack knowledge, digital literacy or sound judgment. Drawing on public health experience, the speaker notes that what people know and how they behave are different things. A review of 11 systematic reviews on social engineering found only two that examined psychological predictors. Knowledge and awareness had the most consistent support, while evidence for cognitive factors was mixed or contradictory.

The speaker then turns to trauma, distinguishing simple PTSD from complex trauma that results from prolonged, human-caused harm such as childhood abuse. She explains how early attachment relationships build an internal model that calibrates trust and threat before reasoning develops. A systematic review by the speaker and a student found that childhood abuse is consistently linked to online harm, both as victimization and as participation. The speaker proposes that altered trust, threat sensitivity, dissociation and learned obedience to authority could shape susceptibility to catfishing, targeted phishing and relationship-based lures. She stresses this remains a hypothesis that has not been tested directly.

For practitioners, the takeaway is that more research is needed before these links can guide controls. The speaker suggests that industry education should pair digital literacy with mental health literacy, and that design solutions should account for users with such experiences. She recommends working with designers on these questions.

talks.title: Enhanced Web Fuzzing: Improving Your Wordlists With Tooling And Methodology
talks.teaser: Shows how tagging and ranking wordlist entries by criticality makes web fuzzing faster and better targeted.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why the wordlists used in web fuzzing often let penetration testers down. The speaker argues that many public lists are sorted alphabetically, contain junk or dangerous entries, include irrelevant technologies, and miss known critical endpoints, such as a debug toolbar that exposes a Python interpreter. Tool defaults matter less than the list itself, and the list should be sized to the scope of the engagement.

The middle of the talk presents a new open-source tool that attaches metadata to each path: criticality, observed count, category, tags and a reference link to a CVE or advisory. Entries can be ingested from CSV files or existing lists, stored in a SQLite database, and generated as lists sorted by criticality and filtered by context or size. The built-in data draws on bug bounty reports, exploit databases, security advisories, Nuclei templates, fuzzing logs and internal engagement findings. In a comparison with common lists, hundreds of critical entries were found to be missing. A live demo against a lab running Symfony showed a discovered endpoint leading to a leaked secret and then to code execution.

The speaker reports five years of internal use, with about 22,500 built-in entries, roughly a third of them manually reviewed. The main takeaways are to review wordlists before relying on them, sort by impact, trim the list to fit the target, and keep it maintained. The generated full list is published for download and updated with each project commit.
